| 2026-04-22 | clean | 0 | no | — | 34 |
| 2026-04-23 | 2/2 failed | 3 | no | 2861s | 0 |

**Floor date for stream-idle pattern: 2026-04-16.** No occurrences in March or earlier April logs. The class is recent.

**Auth-expiry (401) has a separate, older history** — appears in logs from 2026-03-14 onward (03-14, 03-21, 03-23, 03-24, 03-25, 03-26, 03-27, 03-28, 03-30, 03-31). Not correlated with stream-idle. Likely an orthogonal intermittent CLI-session expiry, not a consequence of hang duration. Session B retry policy must handle both classes independently.

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| S90 silent-cascade class repeated for 5 days undetected | 04-16 through 04-20: all auto-enrich runs stream-idled or 401'd, produced 0 events. `daily-enrichment-check.sh` *did* log `"Warning: auto-enrich ran but enriched 0 events"` on 04-18 but the warning only lands in `logs/enrichment-check.log` which has no reader. Clean days 04-21/22 masked the pattern; 04-23 would have repeated silently if 04-20's watchdog hadn't turned hang-durations visible. | **Every new monitor must specify its non-coverage at design time** — see `patterns.md`. S91 visibility monitor watched sitemap/IndexNow freshness only; enrichment throughput was outside its surface. Session A extends S91 with `enriched_last_24h` column + `STALE_ENRICHMENT` marker when 2 consecutive days log 0. |
| Passive CSV markers are not alerts | STALE marker lands in `data/search-visibility-log.csv`, a file the user checks every 3-4 days manually. Strictly better than log-file warnings that nobody reads, but weekend silent-failure windows remain a known gap until an active-alert path (notification / email / chat) ships. | **Declare alert class at design time** — see `patterns.md` "Passive markers vs. active alerts." Active-alert session is separate, gated on the gap biting again. Do not promote passive→active speculatively. |
| SQLite WAL + `{ readonly: true }` = SQLITE_CANTOPEN | `scripts/monitor-search-visibility.ts` first pass opened `data/events.db` with `{ readonly: true }`. Production DB is in WAL mode (`PRAGMA journal_mode=wal`). Reading a WAL DB needs the `-shm` / `-wal` helper files, which SQLite creates on open; `readonly:true` forbids that creation → errno 14 SQLITE_CANTOPEN. Unit tests didn't catch it because `new Database()` in a test creates a fresh rollback-journal DB, not WAL. Live run produced empty `enriched_last_24h` silently (try/catch returned `''`). | Drop `readonly: true` on WAL-mode DBs. Correctness is preserved by the SELECT-only query + immediate `db.close()`. Added regression test (`works against a WAL-mode DB`) that `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` on the test DB before the query — locks out any future re-add of the flag. |
| Monitor assumes `readonly` is free safety | Intuition that read-only flag = no side effects = always safer. On a rollback-journal DB, that's true. On WAL, it changes open semantics and can silently block the read entirely. | For any `bun:sqlite` access, check the target DB's `journal_mode`. If WAL, do not use `readonly:true` unless you've also arranged for the `-shm`/`-wal` files to be pre-created by a writer process. |

## Price-Acquisition Chain Semantic-Fit (2026-04-23, Session 97)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| venue_default price inheritance without type-compatibility check | Devoxx Greece 2026 (`type=tech`) at Μέγαρο Μουσικής Αθηνών (top-3: concert, theater, performance) inherited the venue's classical-programming default (€25, range €15-80) and shipped to production Schema.org `offers.price`. A 3-day tech conference priced at €25 is confidently wrong — AI engines citing the wrong number in `offers` is worse than an absent price. **Third instance of the same class**: fallback chain does not check semantic fit, only structural availability. First was the enrichment classifier substring bug; second was the scraper dedupe on partial title matches; this is the third. The class deserves a named pattern entry rather than being logged as a one-off — see `patterns.md` "Semantic-fit gating." | Gate `getVenueDefaultPrice(venueName, eventType, history)` by `isTypeCompatibleWithVenue(eventType, venueName, history)`. Refuse inheritance when `eventType ∉ venue.top_N_types` (default N=3). Refuse for `NO_HISTORY` venues as the safe default (count is 0 today; new venues with thin history will appear the moment a new source lands). Backfill: one-shot `--reprocess-source=venue_default` flips existing MISMATCH rows to `unknown` (6 rows on 2026-04-23: Megaron exhibitions ×2, dance, show ×2; Ωδείο dj_set). |
| Venue-Lock Type Mismatches leaked at least 2 cases after S71 "fix" | The S96/S97 Step 1 classification surfaced 2 show→concert/theater miscategorizations at Megaron — `Sir John Eliot Gardiner – Constellation Choir and Orchestra` typed as `show` (is a classical concert) and `Τρισεύγενη` typed as `show` (likely a theater piece). `docs/known-issues.md` line 38-44 marks this class as fixed at S71, but the gate surfaced at least 2 bleed-through cases. The S97 gate correctly routes these to `unknown + CTA` regardless of why the miscategorization happened, so the user-facing bug is resolved — but the upstream categorizer drift is a separate issue. **Flag for categorizer audit in a future session — NOT fixed in S97.** | Re-open known-issues.md entry or promote to a distinct audit session. Do not backfill the 2 events' types in the DB without running the categorizer through the full set to understand the blast radius. |
| `price_range` field contains free-text values, not structured ranges | Ωδείο Αθηνών DJ-set row (`453f3524b0060f6e`) had `price_range: "Door price"` — a text label, not the `€X-Y` structured format used for the other 279 `venue_default` rows. Suggests an upstream scraper or chain step writes free-text into a structured field. Did not investigate root cause in S97 (out of scope); the row was flipped to `unknown` by the gate anyway. | Separate session to audit `price_range` field for non-conforming values. Likely candidates: specific scraper parsing a "Door price" label instead of the numeric tier, or a conditional in the chain writing a descriptive string when no numeric range is available. Search scope: `grep -n "Door price\|price_range =" scripts/ src/` plus a DB query for `price_range` values that don't match `^€?\d+-?\d*$`. |
| Commit scope is not what `git status` says, it's what the index holds | S95 commit `f580df806` silently included 3 monitor-extension files I hadn't intended to stage for Session 96. Searched every plausible hook location (`.git/hooks/`, `.husky/`, `core.hooksPath`, Claude Code `settings.json` at both scopes, plugin configs) — no hook exists. Likely cause: an earlier `git add .` or `git add -A` during the session staged the monitor files; subsequent `git add <specific-paths>` calls added more files without unstaging them. `git status --short` right before commit still showed them as `??` / ` M` in the *working-tree* view, but the *index* already held them. A bare `git commit` with no path args commits the index, not what `git status` displays. Required a reset + resplit to un-bundle. | Before every `git push`, run `git show --stat HEAD` (or `git show --stat origin/main..HEAD` for multi-commit work). Compare file count and approximate line-count against the session's Critical Files list. If they don't match, stop and investigate before pushing — rewriting unpushed commits is cheap, rewriting pushed commits breaks everyone's clone. Named check: **"verify commit scope with `git show --stat HEAD` between commit and push, not `git status` before commit."** |

## Wrapper-Misreport / Inverted-S90 (2026-04-24, Session 98)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| `auto-enrich.sh` reported saved batches as failures for 5+ days | `auto-enrich.sh` bucketed batch success/failure purely by subprocess exit code. `claude -p` exits non-zero on stream-idle even when its save-batch.ts subprocess committed cleanly — so every stream-idle in 2026-04-16 → 2026-04-20 was reported as "0 succeeded, 2 failed" / "Events enriched (est): 0" despite the DB containing full exact-match rows. Triggered Session A (monitor work) and a full diagnostic arc before Path C surfaced that nothing had actually failed. Additionally, `TOTAL_ENRICHED = SUCCEEDED × EVENTS_PER_BATCH` (line 366) was a multiplication estimate, not a DB count — even "successful" batches were reporting inferred numbers. **Inverted polarity of S90**: S90 was silent failure reported as success, this is silent success reported as failure. Same class: observability signal divorced from ground truth. | Wrapper now queries `enrichment_log.saved_to_events` per-batch and buckets by DB state. Subprocess exit code demoted to advisory (still logged, but doesn't determine pass/fail). Four-quadrant log matrix: `OK` (exit 0 + saves), `WARN wrapper-misreport` (exit non-zero + saves, the stream-idle case), `WARN new-failure-class` (exit 0 + no saves — theoretical today; if it fires, something is newly wrong), `ERROR` (exit non-zero + no saves). `TOTAL_ENRICHED` now accumulates actual save counts from the DB, no multiplication. See `scripts/auto-enrich.sh` lines 292-307 (RUN_ID init) and 358-395 (log matrix). |
| `session_id` in `enrichment_log` stores a batch-within-run name, not a session identifier | Grep of 14 days of data showed only 3 distinct `(session_id, batch_number)` tuples: `('batch-1', 1)`, `('batch-2', 2)`, `('batch-3', 3)`. Neither column is run-unique; they're redundant encodings of batch-within-run index. Rollback-batch.ts uses `session_id` as a destructive-operation filter, so the name-change can't happen without breaking the rollback interface. **Fourth instance of "status fields decay"** — field name promises aggregation that the values don't deliver. First: `enrichment_tier='stub'` on enriched events. Second: `price_source='venue_default'` on type-mismatched prices. Third: commit-scope drift (different class but same shape). Fourth: `session_id` that isn't. | Added `run_id` as a new column instead of repurposing `session_id`. Run-unique id generated by `auto-enrich.sh` as `$(date +%s)-$$` (human-readable timestamp + PID), exported as env var, read by `save-batch.ts` via `process.env.RUN_ID` and written at save time. Historical rows stay NULL (forward-only). `session_id` is untouched; `scripts/rollback-batch.ts` semantics unchanged. |
| SQLite WAL + `{ readonly: true }` on S98 migration (avoided by prior learning) | Migration script needed to write (ALTER TABLE + UPDATE for backfill). Tempting to open the DB readonly for the projection preview and writable for apply — but mixing modes complicates error handling. Session A already established that WAL-mode DBs work cleanly with a single read-write `Database()` handle; the S98 migration follows that pattern. Not a new mistake, but a test of whether the S91 learning held under pressure. It did. | Open once in read-write mode. Wrap destructive statements in BEGIN/COMMIT with ROLLBACK on exception. |
| CSV migration's "only handle 18→19" guard was too narrow | `migrateCsvIfNeeded` in Session A hard-coded `if (newCols - oldCols !== 1) return;` to safely skip unexpected schemas. Session 98 needed to handle 18→20 and 19→20 simultaneously (some deployments had Session A's migration applied, some didn't). Generalized to `if (toInsert <= 0) return;` with N-wide empty-field insertion at position (oldCols - 1). Zero regressions in existing tests because the 18→19 path is a special case of the general form. | When writing narrow guards that couple to a specific version transition, note the coupling in a comment so the next extender knows to generalize rather than add parallel guards. Naive add-another-guard would have produced two migration paths to maintain. |

## Pre-A Price-Type Normalization + Migration Tracking Drift (2026-04-24, Session Pre-A)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Legacy `price_type` vocabulary leaked past constitution Tier 1 rule for 10,768 rows | Constitution values are `'open' | 'with-ticket' | 'tba' | 'donation'`. DB held `paid=10611`, `free=30`, `door=127` at Pre-A start — all pre-constitution terminology. Primary writer was `scripts/scrape-all.ts` (5 sites emitting `'paid'`, 1 site emitting `'door'`, RA scraper's internal priceType variable). Downstream readers (`validate-ticket-urls.ts`, `backfill-ticket-urls.ts`, `generate-enrichment-brief.ts`) grew defensive `IN ('paid', 'with-ticket', 'tba')` cruft to tolerate the drift. `door` specifically was a data-model bleed: door-only is a CTA/ticketing-layer concept, not a pricing-layer concept — leaking a ticket_url_status value into the price_type column. | Migration 007 normalized (paid→with-ticket, free→open, door→with-ticket + ticket_url_status='door_only'). Writers fixed at source (scrape-all.ts literals + ScrapedEvent interface extended with `ticket_url_status?: string` + UPSERT SQL expanded to write it). `database.ts` added belt-and-suspenders `normalizePriceType()` helper at eventToRow. Legacy-reader cleanup: defensive `IN ('paid', …)` filters simplified now that DB is normalized. `scripts/migrate-price-types.ts` (earlier one-off that didn't handle door) archived to `scripts/_archive/`. **Beyond Pre-A — recommended**: lint/pre-commit hook that fails on literal `'paid'` / `'free'` / `'door'` in `price_type` contexts in `src/` and `scripts/` (currently no automated enforcement of constitution vocab). |
| `_migrations` table out of sync with actual schema state (drift at 4 migrations) | Migration tracking showed migrations 003, 004, 005, 006 as `pending`, but `PRAGMA table_info(events)` + `PRAGMA table_info(venue_context)` confirmed all columns they add (getting_there, what_to_expect, good_to_know, enrichment_status, enriched_at, time_source, image_url, image_source, ticket_url_resolved_at, ticket_url_source) already exist. Root cause likely: manual `sqlite3` shell application of migration SQL without recording in `_migrations`. Runner `scripts/run-migrations.ts` correctly failed closed (would try to re-apply `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` and SQLite would error on duplicate), blocking migration 007. **Protection worked as designed** — the runner refused to run atop silent drift. Unknown when drift occurred (git log on migration files shows authoring dates but not application dates; no audit trail in DB). | Backfilled `_migrations` with retroactive records. Added `applied_by TEXT DEFAULT 'runner'` column to `_migrations` so future runner-applied migrations get correct provenance automatically (runner's INSERT is name-only, so DEFAULT fires). 4 backfilled rows labeled `applied_by='retro_pre_A_session'` with identical `applied_at` timestamp — distinguishable from runner entries by both label and timestamp clustering. Future rule (scope beyond Pre-A): all schema changes go through runner, never direct sqlite3 execution. Optional CI check: list `src/db/migrations/*.sql` vs `SELECT name FROM _migrations` and fail if any file isn't tracked. |
| Pre-existing uncommitted WIP in test setup broke selectDiverseBatch tests before Pre-A | Working tree at Pre-A start had ~13 modified files + 7 untracked (Session A prep work partially staged). `scripts/generate-enrichment-brief.ts` had pre-existing WIP that expanded the SELECT in selectDiverseBatch to include `ticket_url, ticket_url_status` columns, but `tests/generate-enrichment-brief.test.ts` test-DB schema (inline CREATE TABLE at line 34) wasn't updated to include those columns. Result: 8 selectDiverseBatch tests failed with `SQLiteError: no such column: ticket_url`. Diagnosed via stash+restore to confirm the failure pre-existed my Pre-A edits. | Fixed test schema by adding `ticket_url TEXT, ticket_url_status TEXT` to the inline CREATE TABLE. Not a Pre-A-specific mistake but worth recording: when making schema-adjacent changes to production code, inline test-DB schemas need matching updates. General rule — prefer loading production schema (`schema.sql`) into test DBs rather than maintaining a parallel inline CREATE TABLE. The parallel version drifts silently. (Scope: future cleanup, not Pre-A.) |

## S97a/S97b — Migration Backup `.gitignore` Drift + Audit Pre-Flight Filter Gotcha (2026-04-28)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Migration backup files leaked to origin via freshness pipeline `git add` (commit ff8bcaf82, ~150 MiB) | S97a Step 5 created `data/events.db.s97a-backup`, `…-backup-v2`, `…-postfail-snapshot` (50 MiB each) as forensic safety nets for the CHECK migration. `.gitignore:40` covered exact `data/events.db` but no glob for dot-suffix variants. The freshness pipeline (`scripts/daily-automated.sh freshness`) ran its scheduled 08:00 cycle midway through S97a, included the 3 backup files in its `git add` step, committed them, and pushed to `github.com/chrimar3/agent-athens` (2h push due to blob size). Discovered next morning when S97b reload pre-flight surfaced `freshness` still mid-deploy at 10:14 with the offending commit visible in `git log`. | Track 1 Option B: `git rm --cached` the 3 files (untrack going forward, preserve local copies); add `data/events.db.*` glob to `.gitignore`; commit `8a9a65efd`. Force-push to clean history (Option A) deferred — the 150 MiB will ride along with the existing 375 MiB historical DB cruft when a future `git filter-repo` maintenance session runs. **Lesson: any plan that creates files matching a pattern near tracked files MUST verify gitignore coverage in Step 0.** Add to Guard 6 (Shotgun Surgery): when introducing new file patterns, grep gitignore for coverage AND check for existing pipeline `git add` paths that might catch them. |
| Audit pre-flight filter `genres != ''` masked 11,751 of 12,539 rows that would fail the CHECK constraint | S97 audit + S97a v3 plan both used `SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE genres IS NOT NULL AND genres != '' AND json_valid(genres) = 0` to confirm "0 malformed rows" before adding `CHECK(genres IS NULL OR json_valid(genres))`. The `genres != ''` filter excluded empty-string rows — but empty string is NOT valid JSON (`json_valid('') = 0`), so those rows would fail the CHECK. v1 migration applied cleanly inside the transaction up to `INSERT INTO events SELECT * FROM events_old`, then errored on the first empty-string row; runner's catch rolled the whole INSERT back, leaving 0 rows in the new events table. Migration was marked applied (false success). Recovered cleanly from `data/events.db.s97a-backup` (50 MiB byte-identical). | v2 migration added Step 0: `UPDATE events SET genres = '[]' WHERE genres = ''` (semantically equivalent — JSON empty array means "no genres" — and `json_valid('[]') = true`). Cleanup: 11,751 rows updated; CHECK applied; FTS5 rebuilt; verified end-to-end. **Lesson: pre-flight queries for CHECK constraints must test the EXACT condition the CHECK will enforce, not an approximation.** For `CHECK(X IS NULL OR f(X))`: pre-flight is `SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE NOT (X IS NULL OR f(X))`, never an approximation with extra filters. Adding to Guard 1 template parenthetically. |
| `sqlite3` CLI silently lacks FTS5 module on macOS — different runtime than `bun:sqlite` | S97a v3 plan prescribed `sqlite3 data/events.db < migrations/s97a-genres-check.sql`. The system `sqlite3` shipped with macOS doesn't include FTS5; `events_fts` is an FTS5 contentful virtual table. Running the migration via `sqlite3` CLI errors at `DROP TABLE events_fts` with `Error: in prepare, no such module: fts5`. Pre-flight FTS5 smoke test (`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events_fts WHERE events_fts MATCH 'jazz'`) hit the same error during S97a Step 5, which surfaced the issue before any destructive operation. | Switched runner to `bun run scripts/run-migrations.ts` (project's existing migration runner uses `bun:sqlite` which has FTS5 built in). Migration moved from `migrations/s97a-genres-check.sql` to `src/db/migrations/008-genres-check-constraint.sql` to fit the runner's discovery convention. **Lesson: DB migrations on this project must run through `bun run scripts/run-migrations.ts`, never `sqlite3 < file`** — the system CLI/runtime SQLite divergence is silent (CLI accepts the file, fails at runtime on FTS5 statements). Promoted to a `patterns.md` entry. |
| `launchctl unload/load` cycle in S97a Step 3 was hook-denied mid-execution; resumed in S97b under explicit re-authorization | S97a Step 3 set the canonical PATH on all 11 plists on disk (`PlistBuddy` edits + `plutil -lint` clean), then attempted `launchctl unload && launchctl load` to refresh launchd's in-memory snapshot. A permission hook denied the unload/load with reason "shared-infra modification beyond user's read-only verification scope and was not the explicit user instruction in the most recent message." S97a documented the deferral in `specs/canonical-path-reload-pending.md` and continued with Steps 4-8 (none of which depend on launchd in-memory state). | S97b session ran the reload under fresh, explicit user instruction. Pre-flight surfaced 2 jobs running (`freshness` 2h15m mid-deploy, `enrichment` 15m mid-batch) — plan-spec required waiting; polled every 30s until idle (~3 min wait). Then unloaded all 11 (3 reported "Input/output error" — the 3 already-unloaded plists per S89; harmless), loaded all 11 (11 success). Verified canonical PATH active in-memory on 3 sampled plists (one from each prior pattern group). **Lesson: hook-denied actions are scope-bounded to the message they were attempted in; carrying authorization across messages requires explicit re-instruction. Plan-level allowedPrompts don't carry across separate Bash invocations after a denial.** |

## S100 — Bad Events Cleanup: more.com sports + dj_set misclassifications (2026-04-28)

Six user-reported events (3 specific ids — 2 H Hotels basketball tickets, 1 theatre play misclassified as `dj_set`) opened a diagnostic that uncovered 39 sports rows and 49 dj_set misclassifications. Diagnose-then-fix arc spanned two sessions (diagnosis 2026-04-24, fix 2026-04-28) with three planner decision-gates and one Guard 6 surprise that reshaped the fix midway.

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| `location_status='verified_athens'` is NOT a guard against wrong-category content | All 3 user-reported events had `location_status='verified_athens'`. The arena `Κλειστό Καλλιθέας` is genuinely in Athens, so the venue resolver correctly accepted it — but the events themselves are basketball ticket pages, not cultural events. The location filter validates *where*, not *what*; treating a green location_status as full validation conflates the two. | Recognize `location_status` and `type` as orthogonal signals. A `verified_athens` event with `type='dj_set'` at a sports arena is a category bug, not a location bug — and the cleanup query must filter by venue/url/type, not by location_status. The site-display rule (`location_status IN ('verified_athens','pass_through')`) is correct as a non-Athens excluder; do not extend it to "in-scope" detection. |
| more.com `/tickets/sports/` ingested via config-error allow-list (3 places, scrape-all.ts inline) | `scripts/scrape-all.ts:233` listed `categories = ['music', 'theatre', 'sports']` — sports was deliberately included alongside cultural categories, treating the *site's URL taxonomy* as equivalent to *Agent Athens scope*. Result: every daily run fetched `/tickets/sports/`, parsed events, called `shouldExcludeEvent`, and 30+ leaked through the keyword/venue filter (Greek inflection blind spot — see follow-up below). The line-326 type assignment (`type: category === 'music' ? 'concert' : category`) further produced 30 rows with non-canonical `type='sports'` (not in the EventType union per CLAUDE.md). | URL-path exclusion is a category fix at the right layer: see `patterns.md` "URL-path exclusion for source-boundary bugs". Two layers shipped: (L1) drop `'sports'` from the categories array + URL regex; (L2) extend `event-scope.json` with `excludedUrlPatterns: ["/tickets/sports/"]` checked at save time. Both layers needed: L1 stops the wasted HTTP/parse work, L2 catches future regressions if someone re-adds the URL or a different source links into a sports path. **General rule: when adding a new source to the scrape config, every URL in `pages[]` (or hardcoded equivalent) requires explicit per-URL scope verification — don't bulk-include a site's top-level sections.** |
| `scrape-list.json` was a stale config trusted by the original plan; Guard 6 grep caught it before writes | The Planner's first A2 plan instructed adding `excluded_url_patterns` to `scrape-list.json` and wiring it into `src/ingest/import-more-events.ts`. Both targets turned out to be archived: `scrape-list.json` has zero active consumers (all readers in `scripts/_archive/`), and `src/ingest/import-more-events.ts` doesn't exist (only `scripts/_archive/import-more-events.ts`). Active ingestion is `scripts/scrape-all.ts` invoked from `daily-automated.sh` via launchd. Without the Guard 6 grep ("confirm you've grep'd all ingestion entry points before writing"), the implementation would have shipped clean code into a dead-letter config and the daily 1-row sports leak would have continued silently for weeks. | **Verify config-consumer reality before planning code on top of config.** When a plan names a config file as the seal point, grep for who reads it — both in active code and in scheduled jobs — before agreeing on the architecture. If grep returns only archived consumers, the config is documentation, not infrastructure. Recovery here was zero-cost (caught pre-write) thanks to the Planner explicitly listing Guard 6 as a precondition; the lesson generalizes — every plan referencing a config file should include "confirm consumer" as Step 0. The stale `scrape-list.json` was marked `_status: DEPRECATED` to prevent the same trap recurring on the next session that touches scraper config. |
| Diagnostic filters ≠ fix filters (carried into the plan's Step 0 idempotency check) | Initial diagnosis used title-markers (`title LIKE '%H Hotels%'`, non-electronic-music regex) as reconnaissance to confirm a misclassification *pattern* existed → 6 H Hotels rows + 3 Parnassos recitals. The fix plan's Step 0 idempotency check used **broader filters** (`url LIKE '%/tickets/sports/%'`, `venue_name='Parnassos Literary Society'`) — 39 sports rows + 13 Parnassos rows. The "divergence" looked like upstream state had changed since diagnosis; rerunning with the diagnostic filters showed counts unchanged. The plan's broader filters were actually *better* — they're the right scope for a fix because once a pattern is confirmed, the cleaner lever is venue/URL, not the original reconnaissance heuristic. | **When moving from diagnosis to fix, re-examine whether the reconnaissance filter is still the right scope — usually it isn't.** Diagnostic filters optimize for "show me the pattern with high precision" (small, narrow). Fix filters optimize for "delete/update everything in the pattern's class" (broad, exhaustive). Treating them as the same query is the trap. Step 0 idempotency checks should explicitly state which filter class they're using and what divergence between filter classes is expected. |
| Greek inflection blind spot in scope-filter keyword matching (root cause of why 30 sports rows reached saveEvents at all) | `scope-filter.ts:shouldExcludeEvent` already runs at every save and rejected nothing for the 30 sports leaks. Reason: `excludedKeywords` in `event-scope.json` has nominative `αγώνες` but Kolossos titles use genitive `ΑΓΩΝΩΝ` (`ΕΙΣΙΤΗΡΙΑ ΑΓΩΝΩΝ 2025-2026`). `text.includes("αγώνες")` against `αγώνων` returns false. Same inflection trap likely affects other Greek keywords across the list. The venue list also missed `Κλειστό Καλλιθέας` (smaller regional arena, while the list has ΟΑΚΑ/Καραϊσκάκης/SEF). | **Flagged for separate diagnostic session — not fixed in S100.** Different problem class (Greek morphology) than the URL-path leak. Spike outline: sample 30 random rejected events + 30 random accepted, look for cross-contamination of inflected forms in the accepted set. Decide between stem-based matching, lemmatization library, or expanded inflection lists per keyword. **Why deferred:** S100 sealed via URL-path (which is language-independent and orthogonal); the Greek-inflection fix is a separate axis of robustness. Adding it under S100 time pressure would risk regressing the keyword matcher on edge cases that the existing tests don't cover. |

## S99 — Stream-Idle Wrapper Promotion (2026-04-28)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Initial S99 plan assumed single-output-file model that doesn't match the parallel-batch reality of `scripts/auto-enrich.sh` | The plan's wrapper requirements (stdout-mtime watchdog on a single output file) came directly from the spike script which has one process writing to one file. But the production script runs 2 batches in parallel, both appending to the same `$LOG_FILE`. A stdout-mtime watchdog on the shared file fails: batch-1 stalls, batch-2's output advances LOG_FILE's mtime, watchdog never fires. Discovered mid-Step-3 when reading the existing parallel-batch loop. | Per-batch output files (`$LOG_DIR/.batch-${BATCH_NAME}-${RUN_ID}.out`), each watched independently; appended to LOG_FILE on completion. Lesson: **a watchdog wrapper's design must match the topology of what it wraps. Spike topology ≠ production topology unless you verify.** A spike script proves mechanics; only reading the production caller proves applicability. Plan workflow update: "promote spike to production" framing implicitly assumes topology compatibility — Step 0 of any such plan should explicitly include reading the production caller's structure. |
| `--include-partial-messages` is incompatible with `--output-format text` (the existing flag) | Plan said add `--include-partial-messages` "if not already present." The existing script uses `--output-format text` (text mode, not stream-json). `--include-partial-messages` only works with `--print --output-format=stream-json` per `claude --help`. Adding it without changing format would either error or be a no-op. The wrapper doesn't actually need it — server-side stream-idle works regardless of output format, and the existing event-counting mechanism reads from the DB via `saved_to_events`, not from stream parsing. | Skipped `--include-partial-messages` in the production promotion. Existing `--output-format text` retained. Lesson: **flags aren't free additions — they have flag-pair preconditions that must be checked.** The plan's "add if not present" rule needs an "...and verify the flag is compatible with existing flags" addendum. |
| Step 5 verification chain `&&`-coupled to `diff` exit code, masking subsequent commands | The verification block chained `diff /tmp/s99-baseline.txt /tmp/s99-post.txt && echo "..."  && bunx tsc --noEmit`. `diff` exits 1 on file differences (non-meaningful timing diff between baseline and post). The `&&` chain stopped, `bunx tsc` never ran. Misleading "exit: 1" appeared at the end. | Re-ran tsc separately. Lesson: **use `;` not `&&` for verification chains where intermediate commands have non-error non-zero exits.** `diff` and `grep` are common offenders. For "fail loudly if any check fails," collect each command's exit code separately and OR them at the end. |
| `KILL_CAUSE: server-stream-idle` detection relies on grepping stdout for a signature whose exact text isn't documented | The wrapper's post-detection logic uses `grep -qiE 'stream.idle.timeout\|stream watchdog\|stream.idle'` against the per-batch output. These patterns are educated guesses — Anthropic hasn't published the exact log line v2.1.105 emits. If the patterns miss, server-side kills are misattributed (likely fall through to the four-quadrant matrix at line 437 with no `KILL_CAUSE` line). | Document the gap: the patterns may need refinement after the first watchdog-era week shows actual `claude -p` exit signatures. Lesson: **when relying on a third-party CLI's output format for forensics, the patterns themselves are infrastructure that need versioned testing.** Add a follow-up to compare actual v2.1.105 stream-idle output against these patterns at the first observed kill, refine if needed. |

## S100a — Audit Script Tier Logic + Local-Dist Premise (2026-04-28)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| S100a's audit script `tierClassify()` conflated fetch-fail with wrong-@type | The script counted ANY row with `match=false` as "misclassified" for tier purposes. 4 rows tripped match=false: 1 was a missing-JSON-LD page, 3 were HTTP 404. The script auto-classified Tier 1 ("4 misclassified, single-emitter fix"). But none were the GEO hypothesis (wrong primary @type) — all were different problem classes. Manual reclassification corrected to Class 0 (clean) for the actual hypothesis under test. | Future audit scripts must distinguish failure modes in classification logic. **Lesson: `match: bool` is a leaky abstraction when there are multiple ways for a check to fail. Tier classification must read the failure-mode discriminator, not just the boolean.** Logged as a follow-up improvement to `scripts/audit-schema-types.ts`. |
| S100a's original plan assumed local dist had the full 12,300-page corpus; it had 45 files | Plan: "scan dist for 12,300 pages." Reality: local dist had 45 .html files (homepage + hubs + cornerstones + venue index). `dist/events/` was empty. The Apr 28 13:44 build was a partial/skeleton state. The audit's premise was invalidated. | Pivoted to live audit via sitemap (Path B in the status report). Same answer in 15s, no rebuild dependency. **Lesson: any audit plan that assumes a generated artifact's state must verify that state before scanning, not after.** `find dist -name 'index.html' \| wc -l` before sampling would have caught the gap upfront. Future audit plans should include a Step 0 corpus-existence check; if local artifact has fewer items than expected, escalate to "rebuild or pivot" decision before continuing. |

## S100 — Path B Pivot from Auth-Pending Importer Plan (2026-04-28)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| S100 plan inferred existing GSC auth client from S91 monitoring's existence; State C was the actual state | The Constitutional reminder said "GA4/GSC use existing Google Cloud auth," and S91's `monitor-search-visibility.ts` is described as monitoring GSC indexed counts. The plan inferred from these that an API client must exist somewhere. Reality: S91 takes `--gsc-indexed=N` as a CLI flag (operator-typed), not via API. The "monitoring" is HTTP probes + sitemap counts; the GSC count is manual entry. No API client exists. Step 0 surfaced this; the plan's State A/B/C fallback caught it gracefully. | Lesson: **infer existing client/auth state from concrete evidence (package.json deps, import statements, gcloud config), not from vibes-based "this monitoring script must use the API."** Plans that rely on inferred infrastructure should always include a Step 0 grep that proves or falsifies the inference, with an explicit fallback if falsified. S100 plan did this correctly with the State A/B/C ladder; the correct response was Path B (defer to S100b under explicit auth setup), not autonomous credential creation. |
| S100 plan didn't anticipate that the auth-pending importers would dominate session value | The plan estimated "5-7 new files, ~400 LOC." Path A would have shipped 5 files but ~60% of the LOC would be stub error handling for the auth-pending state. The actual measurable value (functional KPI db ready to receive data, baseline anchor for I/O comparison, manual logging template for GEO) lived in Steps 1, 2, 6.1, 8, 9 — which is what Path B shipped. | Lesson: **when a plan crosses multiple data sources behind separate auth/access dependencies, the value-density per step is uneven.** Estimating LOC isn't the right metric — estimating "what unblocks downstream work this week" is. Path B's "skeleton + 5 prompts + baseline" unblocks GEO Strategist's manual logging starting Friday; the auth-pending importers don't unblock anything until next week's S100b session. Future similar plans should estimate value-flow ("Editorial unblocked Friday") not file-flow ("5 files written"). |

## S101a — Brief-vs-reality mismatch: schema premise stale (2026-05-02)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| S101a brief assumed `/this-weekend` was missing `mainEntity → ItemList → itemListElement[]` and proposed adding it from scratch | Phase-0 exploration found `src/templates/page.ts:386-449` (`generateSchemaMarkup`) already emits the full structure: `CollectionPage → mainEntity → ItemList → itemListElement[]` with `inLanguage`, `numberOfItems`, 1-indexed `position`, `eventStatus`, full `location` hierarchy. Verified empirically against `dist/this-weekend.html` (30 ListItems) and `dist/en/this-weekend/index.html` (30 ListItems). The brief's S100a audit had sampled `@type` only — it didn't check whether `mainEntity` was populated. The plan was rewritten to scope-down Step 1 (refinements only) and re-frame Step 4 (extend existing hash to JSON-LD, not add Friday plist). The brief's Editorial Pushback 2 concern was correct — fraudulent timestamp bumps — but the proposed fix (Friday plist) didn't address the actual issue (JSON-LD `dateModified` source was `new Date()`, not hash-gated). ## S101 — Enrichment Drought Diagnostic (2026-05-03)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| 5-day drought went undetected; existing monitoring was insufficient to alert | Last successful enrichment was 2026-04-28; first failed batch was 2026-04-29 16:34. Five days of zero saves elapsed before the user dispatched S101. The `STALE_ENRICHMENT` marker in `data/search-visibility-log.csv` only fired on 04-27, 05-01, 05-03 (intermittent). Slot 19's stderr file had been logging "Auto-enrichment failed (non-fatal, continuing...)" daily since **2026-04-18** (2+ weeks), with no escalation. Saves still appeared on 04-24/04-27/04-28 because *other* slots (13/16/22/01) were succeeding — until 04-29 when all slots simultaneously degraded. | Need a positive-counter alert: `if MAX(enriched_at) < now() - 36h then page`. Sub-pattern: **"non-fatal, continuing..." in a stderr line is a code smell when it appears every day for weeks** — it's not non-fatal at the user-visible KPI level, just at the script's flow-control level. The "non-fatal" designation referred to "downstream pipeline phases (image enrichment etc.) can still complete," not "system is healthy." Lesson: **"non-fatal" must be measured against user-visible outcomes, not script flow control.** If a step's failure produces zero downstream value but the parent script keeps going, monitoring must treat it as critical-path failed. |
| Brief's Class B prescribed fix (revert wrapper to caffeinate -s) was wrong for the actual failure mode | Brief offered a class-table mapping signature → known fix. Class B's signature ("no progress for >TIMEOUT, no error") matched today's logs exactly. The known fix said "revert S99 wrapper to caffeinate -s." But the keystone evidence — every preserved `logs/.batch-*.out` file is **0 bytes** — proved the wrapper wasn't the cause; the CLI subprocess produced literally zero stdout bytes before being killed. Reverting the wrapper would have removed the only thing bounding the damage (processes would hang forever instead of being killed at 121s). | Always verify "messenger vs cause" before applying a class-table fix. Keystone test for stdout-idle-style failures: **read the preserved per-batch output file. If it contains *any* bytes → wrapper killed mid-stream and is suspect. If 0 bytes → wrapper is the messenger, hang is upstream.** Logged as a pattern in `patterns.md`. The brief's safety net (Class G + conditional-continuation rule "B/D/E/G → STOP") caught the wrong-fix risk even though Class B's signature matched. Lesson: **conditional-continuation guards should always include "STOP" for any class whose fix is destructive-if-misapplied**, not just for novel cases. |
| Brief assumed `.claude/notes/session-log.md`; actual path is `docs/session-log.md` | Step 0 of the brief said `tail -5 .claude/notes/session-log.md`. That path doesn't exist; the actual session log per `.claude/CLAUDE.md` is `docs/session-log.md`. Resolved by deriving session number from the latest `specs/s*` filenames (s100, s100a → S101). Also flagged: brief memory said 22:00/01:00 plists were unloaded, but `launchctl list` shows both currently loaded. | Per `feedback_verify_paths_in_briefs.md`, verify path assumptions before running commands against them. Lesson: **briefs that quote specific paths and memory claims should be cross-checked against `.claude/CLAUDE.md` and live system state**. Both mismatches were flagged in the diagnostic spec rather than silently corrected, so future readers can see the brief vs reality. |

## S101a — Enrichment Drought Fix (2026-05-03)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Initial fix (`< /dev/null` + `--output-format stream-json --verbose`) was insufficient on its own; first post-fix run still saw both batches killed at idle=134s/127s | Step 1's foreground test surfaced a `Warning: no stdin data received in 3s` warning that strongly suggested H1 (stdin) was the root cause — and adding `< /dev/null` *did* solve the warning. But Step 2c showed the production-sized 16KB prompt still produced 0 inference output for 90s+ even with the redirect (just the warning text in stderr). Step 2f then proved switching to `stream-json --verbose` produces streaming output starting at byte 10s. Both fixes applied; first launchctl-driven verification (RUN_ID=1777832932) still saw both batches killed: batch-1 elapsed=317s idle=134s, batch-2 elapsed=378s idle=127s. The wrapper's 120s stdout-idle gate fired during silent description generation (stream-json emits per-turn events, but text generation between turns is silent without partial-messages). | Apply `--include-partial-messages` as a third flag (only valid with stream-json per `claude --help`). Adds `content_block_delta` events on every few tokens. Verified: second post-fix run (RUN_ID=1777833477) saved 5 of 10 events; batch-1 fully completed and saved cleanly with `subprocess exited 143 but 5 events saved successfully` (S98 reconciliation logic). Lesson: **the "cheapest hypothesis first" guidance applies to isolation, not application — once isolated, all three flags must apply together.** Also: **the CLI's own warning text recommends `< /dev/null`** — that's the cheapest source of truth for diagnosing CLI-level regressions; check it before reaching for dtrace. |
| First fix iteration didn't predict that text→stream-json would expose a *second* failure mode (silent generation > 120s idle) | Step 2f's foreground test ran for 9 minutes streaming 361KB without hitting the wrapper's idle gate locally — but my local test had a longer watchdog (540s) and was wrapped in a polling loop that touched the file via `wc -c`, which doesn't update mtime. The production wrapper polls via `stat -f %m "$BATCH_OUT"` which only advances on actual write. So the foreground test masked the gap-during-generation issue. The actual gating issue surfaced only in the production launchctl-driven test where the wrapper does the polling. | When verifying a fix that depends on watchdog cooperation, **the verification harness must use the same gate logic the production wrapper uses** — not a "did the file get any bytes" check, but `stat -f %m` polling at the same interval. Lesson: a fix that "works in foreground" may still fail in production if the production-side measurement isn't part of the foreground test. The brief's Step 5 ("Re-run the production-equivalent invocation with the fix applied, in foreground") is correct in spirit but needs the harness to mimic production gating, not just the production flags. |
| `claude` CLI v2.1.122+ added a 3s stdin grace period without prominent release-note signaling (or I missed it) | The version ratcheted from 2.1.121 to 2.1.126 sometime in the last ~10 days. The new stdin-reading behavior in `-p` mode is the difference between "this works" and "this hangs forever in launchd." The CLI emits a polite warning, but only when stdin EOFs *eventually* (foreground TTY, not launchd pipe). | Maintain a known-good-flags file for any production invocation of an upstream CLI. When a new version drops, A/B-test the existing invocation against the new binary in launchd-style env before any production rollout. Sub-pattern: **the canary for a CLI version regression is "did the existing invocation start emitting new warnings"** — check `head` of recent BATCH_OUT files for warning-text-on-stderr after a CLI upgrade. |

## S111 — Pipeline Staging Audit Premise Errors (2026-05-04)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Session 110 closeout flagged `dd47f4519` as a pipeline contamination commit | I observed `dd47f4519` had landed between my source push and closeout push, and I attributed it to the pipeline `git add -A` antipattern. In reality it was a hand-authored feature commit by the user (S110 tier-priority queue ordering) — three explicit files, detailed message, attributed to Claude Code. The fact that I'd just deployed at the same date was a coincidence. | Pre-flight P3 caught the mis-attribution by reading the actual commit (author + message body + 3-explicit-files) before treating it as evidence. **Lesson:** automation patterns are usually identifiable from commit message format (`chore: daily pipeline update YYYY-MM-DD`) and small file counts. Hand-authored work has detailed message bodies and the file-count fingerprint of the actual change. Verify both signals before classifying a commit. |
| Pre-flight audit incident count (2) was an undercount | Audit looked at the most recent two suspicious pipeline commits (adbaef38e, 72ce32c73). The fix-session file-count distribution scan surfaced at least 3 more (5d49315a1 13 files, 4a897a76b 5 files, 937f738de 9 files). Pattern was endemic — most days the pipeline scooped something. Audit's "two incidents in two days" framing implied lower urgency than reality warranted. | When auditing a pattern's frequency, scan ≥2 weeks of commit history with file-count distribution, not just the last few days. The pattern's frequency = the rate at which the developer has WIP in working tree at trigger time, which is roughly daily for an active project. |

## S112 — B-2d Venue Dedup Implementation Errors (2026-05-04)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Diagnostic count (59) anchored Strategist lock; actual count at execution (57) drifted | Strategist Q-B8a Path 3 lock from 2026-05-04 morning was based on diagnostic showing 59 canonical_name collisions. By execution time (afternoon same day), small registry edits had reduced the count to 57. The drift didn't change pattern shape but did change exact numbers. | **Diagnostic counts are pre-decision; operate against current state, not anchor count.** Strategist locks should be revised in-flight if drift is observed; exact-count assertions in commit messages should reflect execution-time numbers, not anchor numbers. The drift is small here (-2 of 59 = 3%) but in a fast-moving registry could be larger. Pre-flight Step 0 baseline-check is the right place to re-anchor. |
| Merge script grouped by exact `canonical_name`, missed 2 case-folded uppercase stubs | Script used `group_by(canonical_name)` to find collisions, matching the brief and Strategist's framing. But two of the 408 records had `canonical_name: "ΣΤΑΥΡΟΣ ΤΟΥ ΝΟΤΟΥ"` (uppercase) when the rich record was `"Σταυρός του Νότου"` (mixed case). These are *different* canonical_names by exact match but *same* canonical_name by `normalizeVenueKey` (case-folded). Script ignored them; normalized-key collision check at validation time surfaced them as 2 extra collisions. Fixed via 2 surgical jq deletes post-script. | When the registry's runtime lookup uses normalization (case-folding, diacritic-stripping, whitespace-collapsing), the dedup script must group by the SAME normalization function, not by raw value. Otherwise the script and the runtime see different sets of "duplicates." Specifically for venue-registry: `group_by(normalizeVenueKey(canonical_name))`, not `group_by(canonical_name)`. The Step 4 normalized-key check caught the gap; baking it into Step 2 grouping would prevent the post-hoc fix. |

## S114 — S101a Editorial Picks Infrastructure (2026-05-04)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Brief Step 5 referenced CSS variables `--text-body` / `--text-small` that do not exist in the codebase | The variables `--text-body` and `--text-small` were specified in the brief's CSS spec for `.editor-picks .picks-intro` and `.editor-picks .pick-rationale`. Neither exists in `src/styles/design-system.css`. The codebase uses the `--type-*` namespace for typographic scale (`--type-body: 1rem`, `--type-small: 0.875rem`). The brief's watch-for note explicitly anticipated this — "If any are missing, the component spec from Design Navigator was wrong and S101a needs to either add the missing variable or use the closest existing one. Report any missing variables in the session report — don't invent new tokens." | Pre-flight check: before writing CSS, grep the variable definitions section for each token referenced in the spec. Substituted closest existing tokens with inline comment annotation (`/* spec referenced --text-body which does not exist */`). Sub-pattern: **the codebase has TWO related but distinct namespaces — `--type-*` for type scale (size/weight) and `--text-*` for text colors** (`--text-primary`, `--text-secondary`, `--text-tertiary`, `--text-muted`). Briefs from external designers often conflate them. Always verify which namespace a referenced token belongs to. |
| Brief Step 3 prescribed composite unique constraint on columns that don't exist on `events` | Step 3 spec called for `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON events(hub_slug, locale, week_starting, editorial_pick_rank) WHERE editorial_pick_rank IS NOT NULL`. None of `hub_slug` / `locale` / `week_starting` exist on the `events` table. The brief itself anticipated this in its decision-tree caveat ("almost certainly do not… [if so] drop the composite unique constraint and use a simple non-unique index"). Resolved cleanly by following the brief's own fallback. | The brief's authors anticipated this — and the fallback path was correctly designed. Lesson: **briefs that contain pre-anticipated decision trees with realistic fallback branches save sessions from getting stuck.** When inheriting a brief that prescribes a constraint, validate the underlying schema before writing the SQL — don't trust spec assertions about column existence. The 30-second `PRAGMA table_info` check at Step 0 prevented a multi-step rollback. |

## S101a-B — Microdata Emission + Validator Scope Gap (2026-05-05)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Validator scope < emission scope: `schema-completeness.ts` enforced numeric-price + availability-presence on JSON-LD only, blind to microdata | Site emits the same `Schema.org/Offer` shape from three call sites: detail-page `buildEventSchemaObject` (JSON-LD), hub `generateSchemaMarkup` (JSON-LD), and hub `renderEventCard` (HTML microdata via `<span itemprop>` + `<meta itemprop>`). Validator's regex at `schema-completeness.ts:170` rejected `€`-prefixed values in JSON-LD strings, but `renderEventCard` was emitting the user-visible `priceText` (with `€`) directly into the microdata span. 11,217 microdata price violations passed every nightly build for weeks before the S101a-A audit caught it. | When adding any FAIL-level validator rule for a Schema.org property, enumerate **every emitter that produces that property** before declaring the rule complete. For Agent Athens that's three sites; missing one means the validator's pass/fail signal is structurally untrustworthy. Action: keep an emitter inventory comment near the validator rule definition (or in `docs/architecture/`), and update it any time a new emit site lands. The S101a-B fix added `validateMicrodata` at `schema-completeness.ts:465` and wired it into `validateAllPages`; future Schema.org rules should be applied to all three surfaces simultaneously. |
| Spec §Q4 claimed `generateSchemaOrg` "has no production callers" — `src/`-scoped grep missed `scripts/` callers | Spec line 38 + Q4 (line 321) both asserted dead-code status. Step 0's verification grep was scoped to `src/ --include='*.ts'`. Two real consumers live outside `src/`: `scripts/run-enrichment-pipeline.ts:45,335` and `scripts/generate-schema.ts:18,74`. If I'd trusted the spec and removed the function, the enrichment pipeline would have broken at the next launch. | When verifying "is X used" against an unfamiliar repo, default to a **repo-wide** grep that excludes only `node_modules`/`dist`/`.git` — never just `src/`. Scripts, config files, codegen, generator templates, and CI YAML can all hold call sites. Specifically: `grep -rn 'symbolName' . --include='*.ts' --include='*.tsx' --include='*.js' --include='*.json' --include='*.md' \| grep -vE '/node_modules/\|/\\.git/\|/dist/'`. The cost of widening the search is ~50ms; the cost of a wrong removal is a broken pipeline at the next cron tick. |
| **Audit-session pattern (not blame on S101a-A):** Q-style "is this dead code" audits must grep `src/` + `scripts/` + every other code path the build pipeline invokes — never `src/` alone | The S101a-A audit grep for `generateSchemaOrg` consumers checked `src/` only and concluded zero production callers. `scripts/` has two live consumers (`run-enrichment-pipeline.ts`, `generate-schema.ts`) that the daily pipeline invokes via `bun run scripts/...`. The audit's finding wasn't dishonest — it accurately reported what `src/` contained — but the scope was narrower than the question being answered. | For any future audit session that includes "Q-style" dead-code checks, the canonical scope set for Agent Athens is: `src/` + `scripts/` + `netlify/functions/` + anything referenced from `package.json` scripts. Audit reports should explicitly list **which roots were searched** so the reader can spot a scope gap before acting on the conclusion. Concretely: prefer `grep -rn 'symbolName' src/ scripts/ netlify/ --include='*.ts'` and document that exact command in the audit deliverable. The lesson generalizes: an audit's confidence is bounded by its search scope, and undisclosed scope is a silent ceiling on that confidence. |

## S116 — Sprint 2 closeout: cross-stream `git add -A` contamination recurrence (2026-05-06)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Concurrent commit `ae0f0d5f1` ("S2: taxonomy hygiene") swept up Sprint 2 sameAs additions while they were staged-but-not-committed in Session 116 | Mid-session, after I edited `config/athens-venues.json` with 3 Tier 1 sameAs additions and ran `git add config/athens-venues.json`, a concurrent commit landed on `main` that included my staged sameAs along with the taxonomy hygiene workstream's files. The commit message did NOT mention sameAs (claimed only neighborhood_aliases + entity-tag filter work). The neighborhood_aliases content the message DID claim was actually in a stash, not the working tree at commit time. Two-way drift: commit content includes things the message doesn't mention (sameAs), AND the message claims things the commit doesn't include (neighborhood_aliases). Detected at Step 4 verification when `git diff --cached --stat` showed 16 files staged after a single-path `git add`. By the time detection happened, the bundling commit was already pushed to origin — destructive unwind no longer safe. Same shape as S111 contamination from the daily pipeline; this recurrence proves the pattern persists across non-pipeline workstreams too. | Accept-bundling-and-continue was the only safe option once pushed. Sprint 2 still closed substantively (origin/main went from `ae0f0d5f1` to `b56bceb0f` — bundled commit + 2 of mine landed cleanly afterward). The audit trail has a flagged-in-retrospective blemish but the end state is correct. **Lesson — the stage-precisely preference is necessary but not sufficient.** Even staging by exact path doesn't protect against another stream's `git add -A` running concurrently. Real fix is at the tooling layer: the daily pipeline (and any concurrent commit producer) needs a guard that detects "files modified by another process within last N minutes" and refuses to stage them. Filed in `specs/sprint-2-retrospective.md` for retro consideration. |
| `ae0f0d5f1` commit message describes content that isn't in the commit (claims `neighborhood_aliases` was added; actual diff has zero such hunks) | `git stash push -- config/athens-venues.json` was run mid-session to isolate pre-existing working-tree modifications. The stash captured the neighborhood_aliases additions. The subsequent concurrent `git add -A` + commit captured what was in the working tree at commit time — which did NOT include the stashed content. The commit message was authored against intent, not against actual diff. | Always inspect the actual diff before authoring a commit message — `git diff --cached` once just before `git commit` catches this. For automated commit-producers (daily pipeline), generate the message FROM the diff, not from a pre-baked plan. The stash content should be flagged as orphaned in stash list and surfaced in next-session pre-flight (running `git stash list` is now part of session-start verification). Recovery path: `git stash show -p stash@{0}` to inspect, then targeted patch-extraction for the desired hunks. |

### Discipline rule — covers two failure layers, not one (added 2026-05-06 post-c0aa81a0d recovery)

The "stage precisely" / "no `git add -A`" preference addresses Layer 1
only. The S2 → `ae0f0d5f1` → `c0aa81a0d` arc proved a second layer
exists.

**Layer 1 (staging-time blob mismatch):** `git add` of specific paths
is necessary but not sufficient. The staged blob =
working-tree-at-staging-time, which may differ from
working-tree-at-edit-time if concurrent processes mutated the tree in
between. Mitigation: `git diff <path>` immediately before `git add`,
`git diff --staged` immediately before `git commit`. Both diffs verify
staging matches intent.

**Layer 2 (verification-time memory/disk mismatch):** in-process tests
verify the in-memory state of the running process, not the on-disk
state of the committed files. After a config edit + commit, run a
fresh-process test invocation to verify the on-disk state matches
intent. Mitigation: separate `bun test` invocation post-commit,
reading the freshly-committed file with no inherited state. See
`patterns.md` → "Memory-Resident State Can Mask On-Disk Divergence
Indefinitely" for the detailed pattern.

The S116 recurrence above involved Layer 1 contamination (`git add -A`
sweep). The c0aa81a0d recovery surfaced Layer 2 (corpus backfill
operating on cached in-memory exclusion set while the on-disk source
had been stripped by an interleaved stash). Both layers need explicit
defenses; precise staging alone leaves Layer 2 unaddressed.

## S110 series diagnostic discipline (2026-05-07, S118)

Five sessions iterated on brief-layer fixes for what turned out to be
a wrapper-layer failure. S110f Step 6 verification fire produced the
empirically clean diagnosis: `KILL_CAUSE: stdout-idle exit 125` at
130s threshold, both batches killed during agent thinking blocks
before save-decision phase ever reached. Two distinct mistakes worth
recording.

**Mistake 1 — Logical-layer fixes cannot address transport-layer kill
mechanisms.** The S101 series chain was: S110 (BATCH_OUT preservation)
→ S110a (lock cleanup) → S110b (config drift) → S110c (parked
IDLE_CAP) → S110e (BATCH_OUT-zero-saves diagnostic) → S110f (brief
revision). Each was correct at its layer. None addressed the
wrapper's `STDOUT_IDLE_CAP` at 130s, which kills the agent during
legitimate thinking blocks regardless of brief content. The agent's
deliberations produce no stdout; the wrapper sees silence; the
wrapper kills. The brief revision in S110f was a logical-layer (agent
reasoning) fix for what is actually a transport-layer (wrapper stdout
cap) problem.

*Diagnostic discipline going forward:* when a kill happens, distinguish
(a) the proximate kill signal (`KILL_CAUSE`, exit code) from (b) the
system layer that owns the kill criterion. Fix at the layer that owns
it. If the agent's reasoning shape is the *symptom* but the wrapper's
threshold is the *criterion*, recalibration is the fix — not brief
revision. This is the meta-lesson that explains why we shipped S101 →
S101a → S110 → S110b → S110c → S110e → S110f and still don't have
throughput restored. Each fix was correct at its layer. None of them
addressed the layer that actually owned the failure.

**Mistake 2 — Bundled architectural + behavioral scope produces wrong
verification gates.** S110f was framed as "throughput restoration"
because the brief revision was the proximate trigger and the relay
chain was: "S110e diagnosed question-stall → S110f revises the brief
→ therefore S110f restores throughput." This framing determined the
verification gate ("≥3 saves"), which is the gate for *behavioral*
work. But S110f's actual scope was *citation-correctness governance*
— validator + chokepoint filter + monitoring + kill switch + override
path. The right gate for governance work is "infrastructure passes
its own self-tests + dangling-ref scan + monitoring renders cleanly,"
all of which S110f passed.

*Discipline going forward:* when a session bundles architectural work
with behavioral fixes, the verification gate must distinguish them.
Specifically:
- *Architectural success* = self-tests pass + invariants hold +
  monitoring renders + dangling-ref clean
- *Behavioral success* = the system metric the change was supposed to
  move actually moves

A session can succeed on (a) and fail on (b); these are independent.
The Dev Planner is responsible for naming both gates explicitly in
the plan, not folding (a) into (b). Future sessions will face this
same shape — bundling architectural work with behavioral fixes — and
the failure to gate them separately will produce the same confusion.

**Mistake 3 — Trace the actual data flow through the invocation line
before designing transport-layer fixes.** S110g Step 1 surfaced the
third mechanism-misunderstanding in the S110 series. The original
plan's Fix B framing assumed the wrapper parses stream-json events
from stdout. Phase 1 exploration corrected that to "wrapper polls
`BATCH_OUT` mtime" — already a one-step trace correction. But the
revised Fix B1 then assumed `save-batch.ts` is a streaming consumer
of the agent's events, which would emit a heartbeat to `BATCH_OUT`.
Step 1's source read corrected that too: `auto-enrich.sh:360`
redirects Claude's stdout *directly* to `BATCH_OUT` with `> "$BATCH_OUT" 2>&1` —
no streaming consumer in the path — and `save-batch.ts` is invoked
*by the agent itself at the end of its session* (per
`generate-enrichment-brief.ts:716`) as a post-batch reader of
`temp-descriptions/<id>.md` files. There is no streaming process to
add a heartbeat to; the heartbeat target was imaginary.

*Diagnostic discipline going forward:* before designing any
transport-layer fix (heartbeat, watchdog, filter, mtime tracker),
read the exact invocation line that produces the signal in question.
Trace stdout → stderr → file-write paths empirically. Identify each
process in the data flow as one of: (a) streaming producer, (b)
streaming consumer, (c) post-batch reader, (d) polling observer.
Match the fix to the role. A heartbeat must be inserted in a process
that is alive during the silence; a watchdog must observe a signal
that the alive process is producing; a filter must sit on the actual
byte path. Do not infer process roles from intuition about how the
system "should" work.

The compounding pattern: each S110-series session took *one* trace
step from intuition toward source. The fix-design phases consistently
failed to take the *next* trace step on the heartbeat-target side.
**Two trace steps per fix is the minimum:** one to locate the kill
mechanism, one to locate the heartbeat / filter / observer insertion
point. Both must be source-verified before the fix is designed. A
plan whose fix taxonomy hasn't been data-flow-traced is a plan that
will produce architecturally-inert "fixes."

**Mistake 4 — Empirical observation: when the kill-idle mode clusters
at the cap, the cap is killing the median not the tail.** S110g's
calibration of `STDOUT_IDLE_CAP` revealed 76/90 stdout-idle kills
landed at idle 120-134s (cap was 120; polling-overshoot window
120-135). Mode was 122s. This is the empirical signature of "cap is
set at the median of natural distribution" — every event that thinks
slightly above average gets killed. The fix at 600s (max-observed-
real-silence 404s × 1.5 buffer) eliminated the failure mode binary-
cleanly: 0 stdout-idle kills in the verification fire (run_id
1778180428-57709, 2026-05-07 22:00).

*Diagnostic discipline going forward:* when a kill-idle mode is
suspiciously close to the cap (within polling-overshoot window),
that's evidence the cap is too tight, not that the population is
unusually slow. The sanity check is "where would the kill-idle mode
be if the cap were doubled?" — if the answer is "much further from
the new cap," the original cap was killing natural distribution; if
it's "still right at the new cap," the system has a real
catastrophic-stall behavior that's symptom-not-cap.

**Vindication of Fix C-revised's honest accounting:** in the same
verification fire, Fix C-revised was in place but didn't have to fire
— the 4 mid-run cases from prior log analysis that I initially
claimed it would catch were actually too tightly-coupled to BATCH_OUT
mtime to need separate observation (Write-tool stream events advance
BATCH_OUT mtime in the same wall-clock second as the file write, so
`find -newer "$BATCH_OUT"` returns nothing in that flow). The
"probably 0 today, kept as defense-in-depth" prediction held cleanly.
The decisions.md entry reflects this truthfully rather than over-
crediting C-revised's coverage.

## S122 — Shared-tree `git push` from parallel session published our commit before authorization (2026-05-08)

| Mistake | What Happened | Correct Approach |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Parallel session's `git push` swept up our unpushed local commit (`b93bff7f1`) and made it public before we authorized it | `git push` pushes the current branch including all ancestor commits between `origin/main` and `HEAD` — does not filter by which session authored which commit. Shared working tree on `main` = shared push surface. | Before ANY `git push` from a session that may run concurrently with others: `git log origin/main..HEAD --oneline` to enumerate what will go public. If unexpected commits appear, decide explicitly before pushing. Long-term: consider `claude/<topic>` feature branches per session — pushed via PR, never directly. (S122, 2026-05-08) |

## S125 — Diagnosed "lost content" from a transient grep without cross-checking multiple signals (2026-05-08)

| What went wrong | Why | Correct approach |
|---|---|---|
| Diagnosed "session-log content lost" from a transient grep that returned empty during another session's stash window | Conclusion drawn from single observation without verifying with multiple data sources (git diff, git log, fsck output cross-reference). Assumed snapshot represented persistent state. | When working-tree state appears anomalous in a shared repo: cross-check via git diff HEAD, git stash list, and git reflog HEAD before declaring content lost. Single grep of a working tree mid-multi-session-day is insufficient evidence. (S125, 2026-05-08) |

**Pattern (third occurrence today):** S122 push-surprise + this entry are the same root cause — assumption-from-snapshot in a shared-repo environment without verifying with multiple signals. Connects to `decisions.md` S125 entry "Verify State Before Reporting".

## S127 — Briefs assumed work surfaces that didn't actually exist (2026-05-10)

| What went wrong | Why | Correct approach |
|---|---|---|
| Brief framed S127 as "generalize content-hash gating to remaining 6 cornerstones"; Phase 1 reconnaissance found only 3 ungated cornerstones actually existed (today, this-month, open). The other 3 (`/tomorrow`, `/this-week`, `/next-month`) were references in template strings, sitemap `dailyPrefixes` classifiers, and audit checklists — but had no `config/hub-pages.json` entry and no built `dist/` directories. | The audit-source citations (`generate-site.ts:1234-1235` template comment, `sitemap/generate-sitemaps.ts:30` changefreq classifier, `ping-indexnow.ts` checklist) read as authoritative because they listed slugs in cornerstone-shaped contexts. Nobody cross-referenced against the canonical hub config that actually drives hub-page generation. | Before treating any slug as a real surface, cross-reference against the canonical config that actually drives generation (`config/hub-pages.json` for hub pages here). Don't accept a slug as "live" because it appears in a template string, sitemap classifier, or audit list — those are aspirational/observational, not authoritative. (S127, 2026-05-10) |
| Brief encoded a Class A vs Class B decision gate based on filter shape: "if a cornerstone uses a non-date filter (Class B), STOP — it needs a parallel hash function." Six occurrences now: S71, S82, S95, S100b, S101a, S132'. | At this count, the failure mode is no longer about CC executors verifying briefs at session start — it's about the Dev Planner's pre-flight protocol. The S132' brief's causal chain was rigorous; the premise it stood on was a stale GSC observation. The 6× pattern shows text-based defenses ("verify before acting") don't survive across plan authoring sessions because the brief gets written from one snapshot of reality, the executor opens it in another, and the verification step is conceptually downstream of the plan that already encodes the unverified premise. Each instance log trained CC; none changed the upstream brief-authoring step. | **Protocol change (not another reminder).** Pre-flight verification rule for the Dev Planner: any defect premise that originated from a screenshot, a single-page observation, or an external-tool inspection (GSC, browser DevTools, Lighthouse) must be checked against current `dist/` or production **before the plan is written**, not after the executor starts. Concretely, for any brief whose headline is "defect X exists on Y pages": the plan author runs the reproduction grep/curl first and either (a) confirms the headline holds and proceeds, or (b) opens the plan with the observed mismatch and re-frames the work. The cost of the 30-second grep is far less than the cost of writing a plan against a non-bug — and the cost-of-being-wrong compounds: executors spend a full session inheriting a misframed premise, then institutional memory absorbs the misframe as if it were a real recurring bug class. The S128 audit conclusion that schema work was "complete" was upstream of this gap. | When an internal pass / external fail disagreement appears: treat the internal validator as suspect first, the production output as suspect second. ## S137 — Single-call-site normalizer regressed within 24h of S136 migration (2026-05-13)

| What went wrong | Why | Correct approach |
|---|---|---|

The 2026-05-13 audit's named-suspect bypass writers (`src/ingest/email-ingestion.ts:322`, `src/images/image-pipeline.ts:34`) were red herrings — neither writes `price_type`. The actual bypass surface was the scraper-side raw-SQL writers in `scripts/scrape-all.ts`, `scripts/scrape-ai-tech.ts`, `scripts/scrape-snfcc.ts`. | "Belt-and-suspenders normalizer" reads like defense-in-depth but only protects the path that imports the normalizer. A single un-exported function with one call site is, despite the metaphor, a single-belt design — and silently so, because the metaphor obscures the topology. A parallel writer that bypasses the normalizer cannot fail any test or build check, since both behaviors emit valid Schema.org and the validator only inspects emitted JSON-LD (where `'tba'` and `'with-ticket'-without-price` produce identical output). | When introducing a normalizer at one write site, also ship its detective control. The detective control should fail the build on out-of-vocabulary data, not on out-of-shape JSON-LD. Concretely: export the normalizer (so parallel writers CAN call it), grep every other writer for the column (so you know which ones to route), and add a vocabulary check in the pre-emission build pass (so the next bypass aborts CI before reaching prod). S137 wired exactly this — `validatePriceTypeVocabulary()` runs against `locationFiltered` in `src/generate-site.ts` before page generation; any future bypass fails the build. (S137, 2026-05-13) |
| Audit (2026-05-13) named two src/ writers as candidate bypass paths based on `grep -rn "UPDATE events"`. Both turned out to write columns OTHER than `price_type` (one writes a dead `price` column from email-ingestion; the other writes `image_local`). Static-grep enumeration of "events writers" is too coarse for column-specific bypass diagnosis. | The grep that finds the bug needs to match the column being normalized, not the table being written. `UPDATE events SET …` matches every UPDATE statement; only some write `price_type`. The audit's reasoning was right (single-call-site normalizers are fragile) but its candidate list was wrong (over-eager scope). | Diagnostic-before-method discipline: column-bypass questions need column-grep evidence. `grep -rn "price_type\s*[=:]" src/ scripts/ --include='*.ts'` is the right tool. Trace each match: writes-to-DB vs reads-from-DB vs config/filter. Doing this would have surfaced `scripts/scrape-all.ts:1407` as the only `'tba'`-producing bypass in 5 minutes, before any code change. (S137, 2026-05-13) |
| **Sibling-field drift, same-day second instance** (2026-05-14).
